items.title: Rise of the Kakatiyas & the Line of Rulers
items.body:
### Rise of the Kakatiyas

**In one line**
The Kakatiyas (c.1163–1323) were the first dynasty to turn the Telugu-speaking land into one kingdom, ruling from Warangal (Orugallu).

**Why it is asked**
This is the foundation of AP/Telangana medieval history — every later Telugu power looked back to the Kakatiyas, so APPSC tests their origin, capital and ruler-order.

**The story (vassals who became kings)**
The Kakatiyas first served as **feudatories** (local chiefs under a greater king) — first of the **Rashtrakutas**, then of the **Western Chalukyas of Kalyani** — in the dry Telangana uplands. As Chalukya power faded, **Rudradeva (also called Prataparudra I)** threw off his overlord and declared himself an independent king in **1163 CE**; we know this from the **Anumakonda (Hanamkonda) inscription**. A telling cultural shift followed: from his reign the dynasty's inscriptions began to appear in **Telugu** instead of Kannada. The capital later moved from **Hanamkonda** to the great rock-fort city of **Orugallu (Warangal)**. The family took its name from its clan goddess **Kakati** (a form of Durga), and its royal badge was the mythical bird **Garuda**.

**Picture it (rulers in order)**

| Ruler | Reign | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) | c.1163–1195 | Declared sovereignty; Thousand Pillar Temple |
| Mahadeva | c.1195–1199 | Short reign |
| Ganapati Deva | 1199–1262 | Greatest ruler; delta expansion; Motupalli charter |
| Rudrama Devi | c.1262–1289 | Rare woman ruler; praised by Marco Polo |
| Prataparudra II | 1289–1323 | Last ruler; fell to the Tughlaqs (1323) |

**Terms explained**
- **Feudatory/vassal:** a local ruler who serves and pays tribute to a stronger king.
- **Inscription:** writing carved on stone or copper — the main evidence for this era.
- **Orugallu:** the Telugu name of Warangal ('one stone'), after its single-rock fort hill.

**Don't confuse**
- **Prataparudra I** (= Rudradeva, who founded sovereignty in 1163) is a different king from **Prataparudra II** (the last ruler, fell in 1323).
- **Kakati** is the goddess the dynasty is named after; **Garuda** is its emblem bird.

**Remember it**
Ruler chain 'Ru-Ma-Ga-Ru-Pra' = **Ru**dradeva → **Ma**hadeva → **Ga**napati → **Ru**drama → **Pra**taparudra II.

**TL;DR**
- Kakatiyas ruled c.1163–1323 from Orugallu (Warangal), shifting from Hanamkonda (Anumakonda).
- They began as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.
- Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) declared sovereignty in 1163 (Anumakonda inscription); Telugu replaced Kannada in inscriptions.
- Ruler order: Rudradeva → Mahadeva → Ganapati Deva → Rudrama Devi → Prataparudra II.
- Royal emblem was Garuda; the family name derives from the goddess Kakati (a form of Durga).
keyPoints: Kakatiyas ruled c.1163–1323 from Orugallu (Warangal), shifting from Hanamkonda (Anumakonda).
They began as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.
Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) declared sovereignty in 1163 (Anumakonda inscription); Telugu replaced Kannada in inscriptions.
Ruler order: Rudradeva → Mahadeva → Ganapati Deva → Rudrama Devi → Prataparudra II.
Royal emblem was Garuda; the family name derives from the goddess Kakati (a form of Durga).
items.mnemonic: Ruler chain 'Ru-Ma-Ga-Ru-Pra' = Rudradeva, Mahadeva, Ganapati, Rudrama, Prataparudra II.

items.title: Ganapati Deva & the Motupalli Charter
items.body:
### Ganapati Deva and the Motupalli charter

**In one line**
Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) was the greatest Kakatiya king — he unified the Telugu lands, built the Warangal fort and the Pakhal lake, and protected traders through the Motupalli charter.

**Why it is asked**
He links three favourite exam themes in one reign: territorial unification, tank-irrigation and medieval trade policy.

**The story (unite, irrigate, trade)**
Ganapati Deva had the longest and most expansive reign of the dynasty. He pushed Kakatiya rule down from the Telangana uplands into the fertile **lowland deltas of the Godavari and Krishna rivers**, bringing most Telugu-speaking people under one crown for the first time. To defend his seat he ringed **Orugallu with a massive granite wall**, ramparts, bastions and a moat. To feed a dry land he had the huge man-made **Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake** dug — one of a chain of Kakatiya **'tanks' (reservoirs)** such as Laknavaram and Ramappa Cheruvu, many still watering fields today. Most forward-looking was his trade policy: at the port of **Motupalli** (in modern **Prakasam district**) he issued the **Abhaya Sasanam** — an 'edict of fearlessness' — promising **foreign merchants the safety of their persons and goods** and charging only a **fixed, moderate customs duty**. This drew sea-traders and made Motupalli a flourishing port.

**Picture it (three achievements)**

| Area | What he did |
|---|---|
| Territory | Extended rule to the Godavari–Krishna delta |
| Water | Built Pakhal Lake; chain of irrigation tanks |
| Trade | Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam protecting merchants |

**Terms explained**
- **Tank:** a man-made reservoir storing rain water for irrigation.
- **Abhaya Sasanam:** 'charter of safety/fearlessness' — a royal promise of protection to merchants.
- **Customs duty:** a tax on goods entering or leaving a port.

**Don't confuse**
- A **brahmadeya/agrahara** grant gave tax-free land to Brahmins; the **Abhaya Sasanam** instead protected **merchants** — different kinds of charter.
- **Motupalli** was the Kakatiya port; it is not the same as the later Qutb Shahi port of Masulipatnam, though both lie on the same coast.

**Remember it**
Motupalli = 'Merchants Openly Trade, Under Protection' — the Abhaya (fearlessness) charter of Ganapati Deva.

**TL;DR**
- Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) was the greatest Kakatiya; extended rule to the Godavari–Krishna delta.
- He walled Orugallu in granite and created the man-made Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake.
- The Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam guaranteed safety and fixed low duties for overseas merchants.
- Motupalli (Prakasam district) was the chief Kakatiya port.
- Kakatiya 'tanks' (Pakhal, Laknavaram, Ramappa Cheruvu) pioneered upland reservoir irrigation.
keyPoints: Ganapati Deva (1199–1262) was the greatest Kakatiya; extended rule to the Godavari–Krishna delta.
He walled Orugallu in granite and created the man-made Pakhal (Pakhala) Lake.
The Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam guaranteed safety and fixed low duties for overseas merchants.

items.title: Rudrama Devi & Marco Polo
items.body:
### Rudrama Devi and Marco Polo

**In one line**
Rudrama Devi (c.1262–1289) was one of the very few women to rule a kingdom in her own right in medieval India, and the traveller Marco Polo praised her government.

**Why it is asked**
She is a rare woman sovereign, and her link to Marco Polo gives examiners both a gender-and-governance angle and a foreign-source angle.

**The story (a queen who ruled as king)**
Ganapati Deva had no son, so he groomed his daughter **Rudrama Devi** to succeed him. She married **Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukyan prince of Nidadavolu**, but she herself held the throne. To command the loyalty of nobles unused to a woman ruler, she took a **male royal style (Rudradeva Maharaja)**. She proved a strong defender: she **beat back invasions by the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri**, and she strengthened the capital, raising her father's wall at Orugallu and adding an **outer earthen wall and a wide moat**. Having no son of her own, she named her **grandson Prataparudra II** as heir. During or just after her reign the Venetian traveller **Marco Polo** passed through (around **1289–1293**) and wrote admiringly of the justice and wealth of her kingdom, which he called **'Mutfili'** — a name taken from the port region near **Masulipatnam** — and noted its diamonds.

**Picture it**

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Reign | c.1262–1289 |
| Marriage | Virabhadra of Nidadavolu (Eastern Chalukya) |
| Defended against | Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri |
| Foreign witness | Marco Polo — kingdom 'Mutfili' |

**Terms explained**
- **Sovereign / queen regnant:** a ruler who holds power in her own right, not merely a king's consort.
- **Mutfili:** Marco Polo's name for the Kakatiya kingdom, after a coastal port near Masulipatnam.

**Don't confuse**
- **Rudrama Devi** (the Kakatiya queen) is not the earlier **Rudradeva** (Prataparudra I) — she only adopted a similar royal name.
- Marco Polo was **Venetian** (from Venice); do not place him with Arab travellers like Al-Biruni.

**Remember it**
'Rudrama ruled, Marco marvelled at Mutfili' — ties the queen to Marco Polo's name for her land.

**TL;DR**
- Rudrama Devi (c.1262–1289) was one of the few women sovereigns of medieval India.
- She married Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukya prince of Nidadavolu, and took a male royal title.
- She repelled the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri and strengthened Orugallu's fortifications.
- Marco Polo (c.1289–1293) praised her rule and called the kingdom 'Mutfili' (after Masulipatnam).
- Lacking a son, she nominated her grandson Prataparudra II as successor.

She married Virabhadra, an Eastern Chalukya prince of Nidadavolu.
She repelled the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri and strengthened Orugallu's fortifications.
Marco Polo (c.1289–1293) praised her rule and called the kingdom 'Mutfili' (after Masulipatnam).
Lacking a son, she nominated her grandson Prataparudra II as successor.

items.title: Prataparudra II & the Fall of Warangal
items.body:
### Prataparudra II and the fall of Warangal

**In one line**
Prataparudra II was the last Kakatiya king; after resisting three Delhi Sultanate sieges, Warangal fell in 1323 and the dynasty ended.

**Why it is asked**
The fall of the Kakatiyas is a turning point — it brought the Delhi Sultanate into the Deccan and set off the Telugu resistance that followed.

**The story (three sieges and the end)**
**Prataparudra II** (r. **1289–1323**) spent his reign fighting off **Delhi Sultanate** armies. An early Khalji raid was beaten back at the **Battle of Upparapalli (1303)**. But in **1310** Alauddin Khalji's general **Malik Kafur** besieged Orugallu and forced Prataparudra to pay a yearly **tribute**; tradition says the famous **Koh-i-Noor diamond** went to Delhi at this time. A further siege in **1318** squeezed renewed submission out of him. The end came in **1323**, when **Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan)** — son of Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** — captured Warangal after a long siege. Prataparudra was taken prisoner and is believed to have **died near the river Narmada** while being marched to Delhi. The victors renamed Orugallu **Sultanpur**, and the leaderless Telugu country sank into confusion under Delhi's governors.

**Picture it (the sieges)**

| Year | What happened |
|---|---|
| 1303 | Khalji raid defeated at Upparapalli |
| 1310 | Malik Kafur forces tribute; Koh-i-Noor said to go to Delhi |
| 1318 | Fresh siege; renewed submission |
| 1323 | Ulugh Khan conquers Warangal; dynasty ends |

**Terms explained**
- **Tribute:** regular payment made by a weaker ruler to a stronger one to avoid attack.
- **Ulugh Khan:** the title of prince Jauna Khan, who later ruled as Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

**Don't confuse**
- **1310 (Malik Kafur, Khalji)** only forced tribute; **1323 (Ulugh Khan, Tughlaq)** actually ended the dynasty.
- **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** was the Sultan who ordered the 1323 campaign; **Ulugh Khan** was the field commander who led it.

**Remember it**
Three sieges '10-18-23' (1310, 1318, 1323) — the third one ended the dynasty and renamed Warangal 'Sultanpur'.

**TL;DR**
- Prataparudra II (1289–1323) was the last Kakatiya ruler.
- 1310: Malik Kafur's siege forced tribute; the Koh-i-Noor is said to have gone to Delhi.
- 1323: Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan), sent by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, finally conquered Warangal.
- Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur after 1323.
- Prataparudra reportedly died near the Narmada while being taken prisoner to Delhi.
keyPoints: Prataparudra II (1289–1323) was the last Kakatiya ruler.
1310: Malik Kafur's siege forced tribute; the Koh-i-Noor is said to have gone to Delhi.
1323: Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan), sent by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, finally conquered Warangal.
Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur after 1323.

items.title: Kakatiya Art, Ramappa Temple & UNESCO 2021
items.body:
### Kakatiya art and the Ramappa Temple

**In one line**
The Kakatiyas built a distinctive temple style whose finest surviving example, the Ramappa Temple, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

**Why it is asked**
Art-and-architecture questions are reliable scorers, and Ramappa is a flagship AP/Telangana heritage fact with a precise year (2021) examiners love.

**The story (stone, bricks and a sculptor's name)**
Kakatiya builders developed clear trademarks: temples raised on **star-shaped platforms**, door-jambs and pillars of **polished black dolerite**, and towers (**vimanas**) built from specially **light 'floating bricks'**. Their landmark monuments are the **Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda** (built by Rudradeva, 1163), the great **Warangal Fort** with its ornamental **Kakatiya Kala Thoranam** (the Kirti Torana gateways, now the **emblem of Telangana**), and above all the **Ramappa Temple**. Ramappa stands at **Palampet (Mulugu district)**, built in **1213** by **Recherla Rudra**, a general of **Ganapati Deva**, and dedicated to Shiva as **Rudreshwara**. Unusually, the temple is popularly named not after the god or the king but after its **sculptor, Ramappa**. Its engineering still amazes: a **floating-brick** tower that reduces weight, and a **sand-box foundation** that cushions earthquakes, while its dolerite figures keep a **mirror polish after 800 years**. UNESCO inscribed it in **2021** (44th session) as the **'Kakatiya Rudreswara (Ramappa) Temple'** (List No. 1570).

**Picture it**

| Monument | Builder / note |
|---|---|
| Thousand Pillar Temple, Hanamkonda | Rudradeva, 1163 |
| Warangal Fort & Kala Thoranam | Kakatiya; gateways = Telangana emblem |
| Ramappa Temple, Palampet | Recherla Rudra, 1213; UNESCO 2021 |

**Terms explained**
- **Vimana:** the tower built over a temple's main shrine in the South Indian style.
- **Floating bricks:** bricks made so porous and light that they can float in water, used to lighten the tower.
- **Sand-box foundation:** a pit filled with sand under the temple that absorbs earthquake shocks.
- **Dolerite:** a very hard dark stone the Kakatiyas polished to a mirror shine.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ramappa Temple (Kakatiya, UNESCO 2021)** is a built-up stone temple — not a rock-cut monolith like the Mahabalipuram rathas.
- The **Kakatiya Kala Thoranam** (gateway) is the Telangana emblem; do not confuse it with the Qutb Shahi **Charminar**.

**Remember it**
Ramappa = 'the temple named after its artist' + **UNESCO 2021**; look for 'floating bricks' and 'sand-box foundation'.

**TL;DR**
- Kakatiya style: floating bricks for towers, polished dolerite carvings, star-shaped platforms.
- Ramappa (Rudreshwara) Temple, Palampet — built 1213 by Recherla Rudra, general of Ganapati Deva.
- It is uniquely named after its sculptor Ramappa; famed for its sand-box (earthquake-resistant) foundation.
- Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 (44th session), List No. 1570.
- Other monuments: Thousand Pillar Temple (Hanamkonda), Warangal Fort, Kakatiya Kala Thoranam (Telangana emblem).

items.title: Musunuri Nayakas & the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
items.body:
### Musunuri Nayakas and the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi

**In one line**
After the Kakatiyas fell, the Musunuri Nayakas led a Telugu revolt that recovered Warangal from Delhi in 1336; the earlier Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi had already given Telugu its first great literature.

**Why it is asked**
The Musunuri recovery is the bridge between the Kakatiyas and the Reddi/Vijayanagara era, and the Eastern Chalukyas explain where written Telugu literature began.

**The story (resistance after the fall)**
When Warangal fell in 1323, the Telugu country was left under Delhi's governors and sank into disorder. Out of this rose the **Musunuri Nayakas**, who claimed to carry on the **Kakatiya legacy**. **Prolaya Nayaka**, ruling from **Rekapalle near Bhadrachalam** (around 1330), issued the **Vilasa copper-plate grant** that mourns the ruin of the Telugu land and presents him as the restorer of order; he died without children. His cousin **Kapaya Nayaka (r. 1333–1368)** then built a wider alliance and, aided (per the Kaluvacheru grant) by **75 Nayakas** and the Hoysala king **Veera Ballala III**, **recovered Warangal from the Tughlaq governor Malik Maqbul in 1336**. Kapaya took the proud title **'Andhra Suratrana'** ('Sultan of the Andhra country'). But he steadily lost ground — including **Golconda** — to the rising **Bahmani Sultanate**, and was finally defeated and killed by rival **Recherla Nayakas at Bhimavaram in 1368**.

**A step back — the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi**
Long before, the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** (coastal Andhra) were founded by **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** around **624 CE**. Their king **Rajaraja Narendra** patronised the poet **Nannaya**, the 'Adi Kavi' (first poet), who began the **Telugu Mahabharatamu**. A Chalukya–Chola royal marriage later produced **Kulottunga I**, who took the imperial Chola throne, merging the two lines.

**Terms explained**
- **Nayaka:** a warrior-chief holding land in return for military service.
- **Copper-plate grant:** a royal order engraved on copper sheets — a key historical source.
- **Adi Kavi:** 'the first poet' — the title given to Nannaya in Telugu literature.

**Don't confuse**
- **Prolaya Nayaka** issued the Vilasa grant (c.1330); **Kapaya Nayaka** recovered Warangal (1336). Keep the two cousins apart.
- The **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** (coastal Andhra, 7th c. onward) are different from the **Western Chalukyas of Kalyani** the Kakatiyas served.

**Remember it**
Musunuri pair: 'Prolaya **writes** (Vilasa 1330), Kapaya **wins** (Warangal 1336)'. Telugu literature starts with **Nannaya** under the Eastern Chalukyas.

**TL;DR**
- Musunuri Nayakas led post-Kakatiya Telugu resistance, claiming Kakatiya heritage.
- Prolaya Nayaka (Rekapalle, near Bhadrachalam) issued the Vilasa grant c.1330.
- Kapaya Nayaka recovered Warangal from Malik Maqbul in 1336 with 75 Nayakas and Hoysala help.
- Kapaya took the title 'Andhra Suratrana' and was killed by the Recherla Nayakas in 1368.
- Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi: founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana (c.624); Rajaraja Narendra patronised Nannaya; the Chola union produced Kulottunga I.

items.title: For Mains — Kakatiyas of Warangal
items.body:
### For Mains — Kakatiyas of Warangal

Mains clauses **M2-2b** and **M2-7** (paper **mains-2**) place the Kakatiyas inside 'AP medieval 1000–1565' and the Deccan dynasties. Argue them as *state-builders of the Telugu identity*, not as a date list.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Political unification | First to join upland Telangana and the coastal delta into one Telugu polity |
| Society | Nayankara system — warrior status open to any birth, giving social mobility |
| Economy | Cascade tank irrigation (Pakhal, Laknavaram) + Motupalli maritime trade |
| Culture | Telugu replaces Kannada in inscriptions; Ramappa, Thousand Pillar Temple, Kala Thoranam |
| Significance/legacy | Model for Reddi kingdoms and Vijayanagara; Telangana state emblem |
| Limitation | Dependence on feudatory nayakas; could not withstand Delhi's cavalry armies |

**Evidence to quote**
- Anumakonda inscription (1163) — the sovereignty marker; Telugu-language shift.
- Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam — a rare medieval merchant-protection charter.
- Marco Polo (c.1289–1293) on Rudrama Devi — foreign testimony on a woman ruler.
- Vilasa grant of Prolaya Nayaka (c.1330) — contemporary voice on the post-1323 devastation.
- Ramappa Temple, UNESCO World Heritage 2021 (List No. 1570) — living heritage argument.
- Cynthia Talbot and Richard Eaton — modern scholarship on Kakatiya social mobility.

**AP angle (natural, not forced)**
The Kakatiya **Kala Thoranam** is the official emblem of Telangana, and the dynasty's tanks still irrigate Telangana farms — a direct line from medieval statecraft to present-day AP/Telangana identity and water management.

**Use in answers**
- Example to cite: the Nayankara system as early 'social mobility' to enrich a society-and-polity answer.
- Quote: Marco Polo's praise of Rudrama Devi for a gender-and-governance point.
- Diagram idea: a Telangana map marking Warangal (Orugallu), Hanamkonda, Palampet (Ramappa), Pakhal Lake and Motupalli port.
keyPoints: Mains M2-2b/M2-7 (mains-2): frame the Kakatiyas as builders of Telugu political and cultural identity.
Strongest arguments: political unification + the Nayankara system's social mobility.
Economy line: cascade tank irrigation plus Motupalli trade via the Abhaya Sasanam.
Culture line: Telugu inscriptions, Ramappa (UNESCO 2021), Kala Thoranam (Telangana emblem).
Quote Marco Polo on Rudrama Devi and the Vilasa grant on the post-1323 devastation.
Limitation: reliance on feudatory nayakas; fell to Delhi's cavalry in 1323.
items.source: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice; Richard Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan; whc.unesco.org/en/list/1570
